extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark (and related non-patent) matters; law firm supervisors responsible for trademark filings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and duties for attorneys practicing trademark law before the USPTO, including signature rules, certification/inquiry obligations, supervision of non-practitioner assistants, candor to the Office, and conditions for discipline and reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of U.S. licensed attorney for foreign-domiciled applicants (U.S. Counsel Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Counsel Rule was intended to (a) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, (b) improve accuracy of trademark submissions, and (c) safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register (84 Fed. Reg. 31498).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and § 11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; and a person electronically signing must personally enter the adopted signature and place it between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission. See 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a),(c),(e) and 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the signature fails to comply because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the submission is improperly executed, cannot be relied upon to support registration, and normally renders the application void (84 Fed. Reg. at 31498; case citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance on signatures (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The person(s) identified as the signatory must personally sign the printed form or personally enter his or her electronic signature; another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign or enter the name of a qualified U.S. signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. TMEP § 611.01(c) emphasizes that all documents must be personally signed and provides examples and admonitions against others signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of improperly executed trademark submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark filings impermissibly signed and filed with the USPTO are improperly executed and normally render the application void; registration may be invalid if signed by an improper person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper signatures adversely affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process; declarations are signed under penalty of perjury and false statements are subject to criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. See cited Fed. Reg. and cases (In re Cowan; In re Dermahose; In re Yusha Zhang).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certifications when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner certifies that statements made on his/her own knowledge are true and that statements based on information and belief are believed to be true; also certifies, after reasonable inquiry, that the paper is not presented for an improper purpose, legal contentions are warranted or nonfrivolous, factual contentions have evidentiary support or are identified as likely to have support after investigation, and denials are warranted or based on lack of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See full language of 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2). Practitioners must be able to support factual assertions by an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to conduct a reasonable inquiry before presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who presents any paper to the USPTO certifies that he or she has conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of § 11.18 may jeopardize the probative value of the filing, and false or fraudulent statements are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001; disciplinary action may follow (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation requiring the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to adequately research or understand USPTO trademark signature rules, resulting in violations in filings, constitutes a lack of competence under § 11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violations include failure to timely notify assistants about an attorney's departure, allowing improper signatures after that departure, failing to take appropriate and timely remedial action to protect clients, and delaying notice to clients and the USPTO about improper signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep clients informed and explain matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep clients reasonably informed about the status of their matters and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit clients to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to inform clients about actual or potential consequences of improper signatures, or failing to advise them until months after learning of the issue, violates § 11.104(a)(3) and (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor to the tribunal / truthfulness (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1), (a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not knowingly make false statements of fact or law to a tribunal (here, the USPTO) and must not offer evidence the practitioner knows to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly authorizing or allowing non-practitioner assistants to use another practitioner's credentials and signatures on documents (including declarations) constitutes making or offering false statements/evidence when those assistants sign in the practitioner's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to take remedial measures for known fraudulent conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must take reasonable remedial measures if the practitioner knows of fraudulent conduct related to a proceeding in which they or a subordinate represented a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to timely disclose improper signatures to the USPTO or failing to stop improper signing after learning of it are violations of § 11.303(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform tribunal of material facts in ex parte proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: In an ex parte proceeding, a practitioner must inform the tribunal of all material facts known that would enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding knowledge that a named signatory was no longer involved in filings (and allowing continued use of that signatory's credentials) violates § 11.303(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b), (c)(1), (c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is responsible for conduct of non-practitioner assistants employed or associated with the practitioner and can be held accountable for violations committed by such persons if the practitioner has supervisory authority, knows of the conduct, and fails to take reasonable remedial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering, ratifying, or knowingly allowing assistants to sign others' names, prepare and file applications without attorney review, or continue such practices after an attorney's departure are specific failures under § 11.503 provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting others in unauthorized practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not assist others in practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing non-practitioner assistants to prepare, sign in the names of others, and file trademark applications without attorney review assists unauthorized practice in the USPTO context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing non-practitioner assistants to sign applications and create the appearance that named signatories signed when they did not constitutes dishonesty/fraud under § 11.804(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, including acts that adversely affect the integrity of federal trademark examination and registration processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: creating thousands of applications that may be compromised for failing to comply with signature rules; failing to conduct reasonable inquiry per § 11.18; failing to ensure attorney review prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compliant electronic signature methods (E-SIGN / H-SIGN) as required alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should use E-SIGN or H-SIGN electronic signature methods that comply with USPTO signature rules rather than permitting others to type or enter a practitioner's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was no justification to forgo E-SIGN or H-SIGN methods which would comply with USPTO rules, avoid harm to clients' rights, and prevent conduct adverse to the trademark registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation that practitioners know and use USPTO resources (TMEP, USPTO webpages, precedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing applicants before the USPTO are reasonably expected to know applicable trademark prosecution and signature rules and the potential disciplinary consequences; the USPTO has published ample information (TMEP, webpages, FOIA OED records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TMEP explicitly states signature requirements; USPTO published rulemaking and prior disciplinary orders provide notice of consequences for similar misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for violations (suspension, probation, public notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the Rules of Professional Conduct can result in disciplinary sanctions such as suspension from practice before the USPTO, probation, publication of the Final Order, and other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case, the agreed sanction was an eight (8) month suspension, probation with specified conditions, publication in the Official Gazette and OED FOIA Reading Room, and waiver of appeal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement and probation conditions (reporting, searches, CLE, TMEP review, boot camp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions for reinstatement and probation include compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, bi-weekly USPTO trademark-searches for filings naming the respondent as attorney of record and prompt written notification to the Office of Trademark Examination Policy of filings made without knowledge/consent, bi-monthly reporting to OED about searches, completion of six (6) hours CLE on ethics/professional responsibility, thorough review of TMEP (including signature requirements), and completion of the USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp (eight modules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must provide declarations/affidavits (28 U.S.C. § 1746) attesting to completion of required education and boot camp enrollment; failure to comply during probation may trigger additional suspension per the Agreement's enforcement provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification obligations for foreign-domiciled clients under suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58 compliance and translated notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspended, a practitioner must comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58. For foreign-domiciled clients who have immediate or prospective business before the Office, required notices (including a copy of the Final Order) may be emailed in the client's native language to client email addresses the practitioner reasonably believes the client directly controls, or to referring entities only if the practitioner takes reasonable measures to ensure forwarding and provides a translated Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific conditions articulate acceptable recipients and precautions to ensure clients receive translated notices; improper reliance on intermediary addresses is disallowed unless steps are taken to ensure client receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and reporting obligations during probation
rubrics_metrics.description: While on probation, the respondent must (a) at least bi-weekly search the USPTO online trademark search system for applications identifying her as attorney of record and promptly inform in writing the Office of Trademark Examination Policy of any filings made without her knowledge or consent; and (b) at least bi-monthly submit a written report to OED confirming completion of searches and any notifications sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These monitoring/reporting duties are express conditions of probation to detect and remediate unauthorized use of attorney credentials in filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations/affidavits under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 for reinstatement attestations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement or probation, the respondent must provide declarations, affidavits, or statements in compliance with 28 U.S.C. § 1746 verifying completion of CLE, boot camp, and review of the TMEP/signature provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signed, sworn statements are required evidence that the respondent completed mandated remedial education and review.
